section: Passive Cooling for Hypoxic Ischemic Encephalopathy

scope.population: Newborn infants ≥35 weeks' gestation with moderate-to-severe HIE, or possible or suspected HIE at the referral stage, awaiting transport from a non-cooling center. Lines that name gestational age, birth weight or postnatal age apply to the group named.
scope.topic: Starting and monitoring passive cooling, and the supportive care and eligibility decisions around it, at a non-cooling center until transport to a cooling center.

claims.manual_text: Infants greater than or equal to 35 weeks gestation diagnosed with Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) are treated with whole-body cooling to a core temperature of 33.5 degrees Celsius, as a neuroprotective therapy.
claims.summary: Whole-body cooling to 33.5°C is the trial-tested method [Shankaran2005][Azzopardi2009][Jacobs2011] and guideline targets sit around it at 33.5 ± 0.5°C, 33–34°C and 33.5–34.5°C [Lemyre2018][Ancora2026][Zanelli2026], but benefit is established for moderate-to-severe HIE at ≥36 0/7 weeks [Zanelli2026], not as routine care at 35 weeks [AAPNews2026][BAPM2025].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests benefit is established for moderate-to-severe HIE at ≥36 0/7 weeks [Zanelli2026]. At 35 weeks, the AAP's lay news summary of its 2026 report describes inconclusive evidence and selective use with families [AAPNews2026], and the BAPM framework advises normothermia below 36 weeks [BAPM2025].

evidence.quote: Therapeutic hypothermia to a temperature of 33.5 to 34.5 °C initiated within 6 hours of birth and continued for 72 hours reduces the risk of death or moderate-to-severe neurodevelopmental impairments in neonates with moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) born at ≥36 0/7 weeks of gestation.

is also not recommended for preterm infants born less than 36 weeks' gestation. For those born at 35 weeks, studies have not demonstrated conclusive benefit or harm from this therapy, and clinicians in select cases may decide with families to use therapeutic hypothermia.
evidence.location: AAP lay news item, What the latest research shows

evidence.quote: Until further evidence emerges, infants born before 36 weeks gestation who develop neonatal encephalopathy should be managed with supportive intensive care and normothermia.
evidence.location: Infants less than 36 weeks gestation; March 2025 update

evidence.quote: The optimal rectal or esophageal temperature appears to be 33.5°C ± 0.5°C for whole body cooling and 34.5°C ± 0.5°C for selective head cooling.
evidence.location: What is the target temperature to be reached?

evidence.quote: Systemic Hypothermia: cools the entire body to a rectal temperature of 33–34 °C
whole-body cooling to an esophageal temperature of 33.5 degrees C for 72 hours, followed by slow rewarming
We compared intensive care plus cooling of the body to 33.5 degrees C for 72 hours and intensive care alone.
Whole-body hypothermia to 33.5°C for 72 hours or standard care (37°C).

claims.manual_text: Initiation of active cooling should occur ideally before 6 hours of age, at a designated cooling center.
claims.summary: Starting before 6 hours and as early as possible is supported [Jacobs2013][Thoresen2013], but guidelines differ on where active cooling begins: CPS provides hypothermia in tertiary units, with passive cooling started in community hospitals before transport [Lemyre2018], while the BAPM framework expects all neonatal units to be able to start servo-controlled cooling [BAPM2025].

evidence.quote: Hypothermia should be instituted in term and late preterm infants with moderate‐to‐severe hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy if identified before six hours of age.
Starting cooling before 3 h of age in surviving asphyxiated newborns is safe and significantly improves motor outcome. Cooling should be initiated as soon as possible after birth in eligible infants.
Therapeutic hypothermia should be provided in tertiary neonatal units and initiated in consultation with a level 3 neonatologist before transport.

While awaiting transport to a tertiary care unit, initiation of passive cooling (e.g., removing the infant’s hat, blanket and turning off an overhead warmer) should be strongly considered in community hospitals, following consultation with a receiving neonatologist.
All Special Care Units (SCUs), Local Neonatal Units (LNUs) and NICUs should be able to assess infants and instigate TH using aEEG and servo controlled cooling equipment as outlined above.

claims.manual_text: The cool body temperature is maintained for 72 hours and then the infant is re-warmed over a 6-hour period (re-warming period may be extended due to instability).
claims.summary: At cooling centers, the setting this line describes, 72 hours of cooling with rewarming over 6 to 12 hours is the CPS recommendation [Lemyre2018], the 2026 Italian guideline sets 0.5°C per hour over at least 4 hours [Ancora2026], and delaying, slowing or reversing rewarming is described for seizures or worsening encephalopathy [BAPM2025][Ancora2026][Lemyre2018]; no retrieved source names instability in general as a reason.

evidence.quote: Therapeutic hypothermia should be continued for 72 hours, with a target rectal (or esophageal) temperature of 33°C to 34°C for whole body cooling, or 34°C to 35°C for selective head cooling. Rewarming should occur over 6 to 12 hours (0.5°C every 1 to 2 hours). Recommendation grade A.
Seizures and worsening of clinical encephalopathy upon rewarming have been reported (35). In such circumstances, experts suggest recooling for 24 hours and resuming rewarming (36).
evidence.location: How should the infant be rewarmed?

evidence.quote: Rewarming begins after 72 hours of cooling, increasing temperature by 0.5 °C per hour over at least 4 hours. High level evidence. Strong recommendation
If seizures occur, prolonging hypothermia for 4–12 hours may be necessary, depending on seizure characteristics and the clinical scenario.
Re-warming can be delayed or slowed where seizures emerge.

claims.manual_text: Infants will not be actively cooled. Only passive cooling will be done while the baby is awaiting transport to appropriate facility.
claims.summary: For infants awaiting transport from a non-cooling center, CPS advises passive cooling and warns against ice packs or cool gels used by untrained staff [Lemyre2018], the 2026 Italian guideline accepts passive cooling when servo-controlled cooling is unavailable [Ancora2026], and BAPM expects transport services to provide servo-controlled cooling in the referring unit [BAPM2025]; during transport, servo-controlled cooling kept more infants in the target range, on low-certainty evidence [Sibrecht2023], and a UK network reported better temperature management after adding active cooling on transport and at referring centers, though short-term NICU outcomes did not differ [Mistry2026].

evidence.quote: While awaiting transport to a tertiary care unit, initiation of passive cooling (e.g., removing the infant’s hat, blanket and turning off an overhead warmer) should be strongly considered in community hospitals, following consultation with a receiving neonatologist.
The use of ice packs or cool gels by untrained personnel, which can lead to severe hypothermia, is not recommended.
If servo-controlled cooling is unavailable, passive hypothermia can be used. High-level evidence. Strong recommendation
All transport services should be able to provide active servo-controlled cooling treatment in both the referring unit and during transportation.

Compared with the other cooling methods, servo-controlled active cooling was more likely to maintain body temperature within the target range of 33°C-34°C on arrival at a neonatal intensive care unit: odds ratio 13.58, 95% confidence interval 4.32-42.66
The certainty of evidence was low.

Compared with passive cooling, the introduction of transport and referring centre active TH improves temperature management of transferred infants with HIE, with more reaching therapeutic temperature within 6 h and fewer being overcooled.
Outcomes for infants were not different.

claims.manual_text: If therapeutic hypothermia is being utilized outside of the set criteria, the risks and benefits will be discussed with the family prior to using this treatment modality.
claims.summary: Guidance ties cooling outside standard criteria to a discussion of benefit and risk with parents [Lemyre2018][Ancora2026][BAPM2025], although the 2026 Italian guideline limits some such cases, including age over 6 hours and postnatal collapse, to research [Ancora2026].

evidence.quote: therapeutic hypothermia may still be considered after discussion with parents, always recognizing the uncertainty with regards to its benefits and considering possible side effects

evidence.quote: In such cases, therapeutic hypothermia may be considered after careful discussion with the parent or guardian of possible benefit and associated risk.

evidence.quote: It is recommended that decision-making involves a second senior person, and that the decision is taken in conjunction with the parents with an explanation of the potential risks and benefits.

claims.manual_text: **Infants will be evaluated for therapeutic hypothermia therapy based on inclusion criteria of:** Gestational age greater than or equal to 35 weeks / **Exclusion Criteria for initiating therapeutic hypothermia includes:** Gestational age less than 35 weeks.
claims.summary: Exclusion below 35 weeks is supported [Lemyre2018][ElDib2026] and CPS 2018 still considers infants at 35 weeks [Lemyre2018], but after the 33–35-week trial [Faix2025], 35 weeks is treated as a selective decision [AAPNews2026][Ancora2026][ElDib2026] or a reason for normothermia [BAPM2025].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests benefit is established from 36 0/7 weeks [Zanelli2026]. A randomized trial at 33 to 35 weeks did not reduce death or disability, with a 74% probability of increased death or disability, and its 48 infants at 35 weeks gave no support for cooling at that age [Faix2025]. The AAP's lay news summary and the 2026 Italian guideline describe 35 weeks as a selective decision with families [AAPNews2026][Ancora2026]; the BAPM framework advises normothermia below 36 weeks [BAPM2025].

evidence.quote: born at ≥36 0/7 weeks of gestation
Bayesian analysis with neutral prior indicated 74% probability of increased death or disability and 87% probability of increased death with hypothermia.
Among infants 33 to 35 weeks’ gestation with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, hypothermia at less than 6 hours’ age did not reduce death or disability at 18 to 22 months’ corrected age.
Our findings for 48 infants born at 35 weeks’ GA provide no support for hypothermia at that GA.

is also not recommended for preterm infants born less than 36 weeks' gestation. For those born at 35 weeks, studies have not demonstrated conclusive benefit or harm from this therapy, and clinicians in select cases may decide with families to use therapeutic hypothermia.
evidence.location: AAP lay news item; summary of the AAP report

evidence.quote: Therapeutic hypothermia may be beneficial, with a weak/conditional recommendation, in case of newborns of 35 weeks of gestational age, when Criteria A, B, and C are all strong.
TH may remain appropriate for select 35 weeks' GA infants, but routine use in 34 weeks' GA and earlier infants should be limited to research settings.
Until further evidence emerges, infants born before 36 weeks gestation who develop neonatal encephalopathy should be managed with supportive intensive care and normothermia.

evidence.quote: Infants ≥35 weeks GA with moderate-to-severe HIE who meet other inclusion criteria should be considered for therapeutic hypothermia. Recommendation grade B.
evidence.location: Summary of recommendations; 2018 statement predates Faix2025

evidence.quote: Therapeutic hypothermia in infants younger than 35 weeks is not recommended. Recommendation grade C.

evidence.quote: In addition to gestational age, a minimum weight threshold of 1800 g was consistently identified in the various guidelines reviewed.

claims.summary: Six hours is the standard limit [Zanelli2026]; for later starts, a trial at 6 to 24 hours in infants at 36 weeks or later gave a 76% posterior probability of reduced death or disability [Laptook2017] and BAPM, CPS and the AAP's lay news summary leave room for cooling beyond 6 hours [BAPM2025][Lemyre2018][AAPNews2026], whereas the 2026 Italian guideline limits it to research [Ancora2026]; the evidence covers starts up to 24 hours only [Laptook2017][AAPNews2026].

Bayesian analysis using a neutral prior indicated a 76% posterior probability of reduced death or disability with hypothermia relative to the noncooled group

evidence.quote: in rare cases where this does not happen within 6 hours, in the absence of evidence of harm or other available treatments, clinicians may decide to administer hypothermia in this context.

claims.manual_text: **Infants will be evaluated for therapeutic hypothermia therapy based on inclusion criteria of:** Absence of an obvious and apparent disorder incompatible with survival / **Exclusion Criteria for initiating therapeutic hypothermia includes:** Presence of known chromosomal anomalies or severe congenital anomalies/syndromes/known metabolic disorders, as determined by the neonatologist.
claims.summary: Trials excluded infants with chromosomal or major congenital abnormalities [Jacobs2013][Azzopardi2008], but CPS limits the exclusion to infants for whom no further aggressive treatment is planned [Lemyre2018], the 2026 Italian guideline confirms contraindications only for severe intracranial hemorrhage [Ancora2026], and no retrieved source names known metabolic disorders.
claims.note: Current evidence suggests the exclusion in CPS guidance covers moribund infants or those with major congenital or genetic abnormalities for whom no further aggressive treatment is planned [Lemyre2018]. The 2026 Italian guideline states that available evidence confirms contraindications only for severe intracranial hemorrhages [Ancora2026].

evidence.quote: Therapeutic hypothermia should not be offered for the following patients: moribund infants or infants with major congenital or genetic abnormalities for whom no further aggressive treatment is planned, infants with severe intrauterine growth restriction or clinically significant coagulopathy, or infants with evidence of severe head trauma or intracranial bleeding. Recommendation grade A.

Some studies suggest potential exclusions, including terminal condition, major congenital anomalies, severe coagulation disorders, and intracranial hemorrhages [32, 53–55]. Available evidence confirms contraindications only for severe intracranial hemorrhages [32].
Major congenital abnormalities, such as diaphragmatic hernia requiring ventilation, or congenital abnormalities suggestive of chromosomal anomaly or other syndromes that include brain dysgenesis
had chromosomal or major congenital abnormalities

claims.manual_text: **Infants will be evaluated for therapeutic hypothermia therapy based on inclusion criteria of:** Physiologic criteria including a major perinatal event - Refer to @sec-clinical-biochem-eval Neurologic exam criteria - Refer to @sec-ne
claims.summary: Eligibility built on evidence of perinatal hypoxia-ischemia plus encephalopathy is the structure used in guidelines and trials [BAPM2025][Ancora2026][Shankaran2005], a recognized perinatal event is never a mandatory element [Proietti2024], and BAPM adds an aEEG criterion [BAPM2025]; the thresholds sit in the cross-referenced sections and are not judged here.

evidence.quote: This involves meeting three criteria: At least one ‘A’ criterion indicating significant perinatal hypoxia-ischaemia, fulfil ‘B’ criterion representing the presence of significant neonatal encephalopathy, and at least one ‘C’ criterion showing seizures or abnormal background activity on amplitude integrated electroencephalography (aEEG)
Once a newborn is identified at risk for significant peripartum asphyxia, it becomes imperative to assess whether it has led to neurological impairment.
with either severe acidosis or perinatal complications and resuscitation at birth and who had moderate or severe encephalopathy
A history of a clearly recognized perinatal event is sometimes included, although never a mandatory element for the definition of perinatal HI.
evidence.location: Criteria indicating evidence of acute perinatal hypoxia/ischemia

claims.manual_text: **Exclusion Criteria for initiating therapeutic hypothermia includes:** Evidence of head trauma or skull fracture causing major intracranial hemorrhage. Intractable coagulopathy with active bleeding.
claims.summary: Severe head trauma, intracranial bleeding and clinically significant coagulopathy are CPS exclusions [Lemyre2018], severe intracranial hemorrhage is the one contraindication the 2026 Italian guideline confirms [Ancora2026], and laboratory coagulopathy alone is expected during cooling, with only active bleeding needing treatment [Forman2014][BAPM2025].

evidence.quote: infants with clinically significant coagulopathy; and infants with evidence of severe head trauma or intracranial bleeding. Isolated intraventricular hemorrhage may not constitute an absolute contra-indication; however, this guidance is based on very limited evidence (26).
evidence.location: Which infants should not receive hypothermia?

evidence.quote: Available evidence confirms contraindications only for severe intracranial hemorrhages [32].
Coagulopathy is physiological in TH but only active bleeding needs treatment.
Laboratory evidence of coagulopathy is universal in HIE babies undergoing TH.

claims.manual_text: **Exclusion Criteria for initiating therapeutic hypothermia includes:** Parent refusal.
claims.summary: A single regional Canadian referring-center passive cooling guideline starts cooling only if parents consent [EasternHealth2022], and BAPM does not require formal written consent but asks that parents be fully informed and their views taken into account [BAPM2025].

evidence.quote: the referring physician should discuss the option of cooling with the parents and if consent obtained initiate passive cooling at the direction of the Neonatologist.
evidence.location: Assessment and Referral, step 5; regional guideline

evidence.quote: Given the proven benefit of TH and its safety, formal written parental consent is not considered necessary, but it is important that parents are as fully informed as possible and their views taken into account.

claims.manual_text: Transports for potential/actual therapeutic hypothermia are emergent.
claims.summary: The 2026 Italian guideline makes urgent transfer mandatory when the birth center cannot provide hypothermia [Ancora2026], the AAP abstract calls for prompt transfer of infants with moderate-to-severe HIE [Zanelli2026], and BAPM says starting cooling in a local unit must not delay transfer, with uplift transfers of infants already cooled prioritised by clinical need [BAPM2025].

evidence.quote: If the birth center lacks therapeutic hypothermia capabilities, urgent transfer is mandatory

therapeutic hypothermia centers should work with their referring hospitals, birthing centers and practitioners to implement educational programs that focus on the identification, initial clinical management of affected neonates, and prompt transfer of neonates with moderate-to-severe HIE.
Commencing TH and/or neurophysiological assessment with aEEG, in a SCU or LNU, must not delay transfer.
These uplift transfers should be prioritised according to clinical need and follow local and national transport service guidance regarding timeliness of transfer (30).
evidence.location: Network and transport implications; infants in whom TH has been initiated

claims.manual_text: Call the identified Kaiser Permanente cooling center for any infant that has a history of acute perinatal event / at risk for HIE according to the hypothermia protocol sheet (refer to @sec-clinical-biochem-eval).
claims.summary: Early consultation with a neonatologist or network NICU for infants with suspected HIE, read here as infants at gestational ages in the cooling range, is recommended [Lemyre2018][BAPM2025], delivery sites are expected to have transfer plans [Zanelli2026], and in one cohort waiting for tertiary advice was associated with a 50 minute delay in the median start of cooling [Lemyre2017].

evidence.quote: Community physicians caring for infants with suspected HIE for whom therapeutic hypothermia is considered, should consult a neonatologist regarding initiation of passive cooling as soon as possible after birth.
There should be early discussion with a network NICU and, where appropriate, network transport services.

Any center or practitioner involved in newborn deliveries should have action plans for prompt recognition and initiation of therapeutic hypothermia or transfer of infants with possible HIE to a center providing therapeutic hypothermia.
Waiting for advice from a tertiary care NICU was independently associated with a 50 minute delay in the median time of initiation of TH.

claims.manual_text: Document core (rectal/esophageal) temperature every 15 minutes. Continuous rectal/esophageal monitoring can be performed with a soft probe inserted into the patient and attached to the monitor.
claims.summary: Core temperature checks every 15 minutes or continuous monitoring are recommended during passive cooling [Lemyre2018][Ancora2026][BAPM2025][Hallberg2009]; in cooling-center cohorts, rectal monitoring had lower odds of overcooling than esophageal monitoring [Wu2024] and esophageal readings ran a median 0.8°C above rectal during cooling [Sarkar2013].

evidence.quote: Rectal temperature or, if not possible, axillary temperature should be monitored every 15 minutes to ensure the infant’s temperature does not decrease below 33°C.
rectal temperature should be maintained at 35 °C, monitored continuously or every 15 minutes
Infants starting any form of TH, including switching the resuscitaire heater off, should have their temperature continuously monitored ideally using an intracorporeal (e.g. rectal) temperature probe.
continuous monitoring of the central temperature is mandatory when such a strategy is used.

Infants treated with TH and rectal temperature monitoring had lower odds of overcooling (OR 0.52, 95%CI 0.34, 0.80) and lower odds of hypotension (OR 0.57, 95%CI 0.39, 0.84) compared with those with esophageal temperature monitoring.
Esophageal temperature was significantly higher compared with simultaneous rectal temperature during cooling, with a temperature gradient ranging from 0.46 to 1.03°C (median, 0.8°C; IQR, 0.6-0.8°C).

claims.manual_text: The temperature goal is 33.5°C–34.0°C.
claims.summary: Published ranges are 33–34°C for cooling and transport [Lemyre2018][Akula2015], 33.5–34.5°C in the AAP abstract [Zanelli2026], a 33.5°C floor for passive hypothermia during assessment [BAPM2025], and about 35°C before hypothermia is started [Ancora2026][Nguyen2025].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests wider target ranges of 33°C to 34°C [Lemyre2018] or 33.5 to 34.5 °C [Zanelli2026], with a floor of 33.5°C for passive hypothermia during assessment [BAPM2025]. Before hypothermia is started, the 2026 Italian guideline keeps rectal temperature at about 35 °C [Ancora2026], and a French Delphi consensus supported 35-35.5 °C for passive hypothermia in the delivery room [Nguyen2025].

evidence.quote: Therapeutic hypothermia should be continued for 72 hours, with a target rectal (or esophageal) temperature of 33°C to 34°C for whole body cooling
The primary outcome was the percentage of temperatures in target range (33°-34°C) during transport.

For newborns ≥ 36 weeks of gestational age requiring Criterion C evaluation, passive cooling must be initiated immediately by switching off warming devices and maintaining a rectal temperature of ~35 °C.

claims.summary: A distal esophageal position appears in one trial's Methods [Faix2025], and the distal-third position with radiographic confirmation only in one study's Discussion [Wu2024]; no retrieved source tests or describes the nares-earlobe-xiphoid measurement in newborns.

evidence.quote: Esophageal temperature measurement is performed by insertion of a temperature probe into the distal third of the esophagus, often necessitating radiographic confirmation.(31)
all infants underwent placement of a temperature monitoring probe in the distal esophagus.

claims.manual_text: Rectal probe: Insert lubricated 5 cm into the rectum Tape to infant’s upper inner thigh to secure
claims.summary: The 2026 Italian guideline places the rectal probe 5–6 cm inside the anal orifice [Ancora2026], a neonatal thermometry review reports a constant reading only at 5 cm [Lei2021], and one cohort report describes 3 to 4 cm [Wu2024]; no retrieved source addresses lubrication or taping to the thigh.

evidence.quote: Continuous rectal temperature monitoring is required, with the probe placed 5–6 cm inside the anal orifice.
Rectal temperatures vary depending on how deep into the rectum the probe is inserted and only reach a constant temperature at a depth of 5 cm (33).
The temperature probe is inserted 3 to 4cm through the anus without need for radiographic confirmation.

claims.manual_text: Monitor core probe (esophageal or rectal) placement Q1 hour
claims.summary: None of the guideline or trial protocol texts retrieved gives an interval for checking probe position, so this remains a local practice choice.

claims.manual_text: For passive cooling measures: once resuscitation measures are complete, the heat source should be adjusted to achieve the core temperature goal of 33.5°C–34.0°C. Ensure continuous temperature monitoring is in place via rectal/esophageal core probe and document every 15 minutes. Active warming devices (radiant heater or incubator) can be turned off to maintain temperature between 33.5°C–34.0°C.

claims.note: Current evidence suggests published aims of 33°C to 34°C [Lemyre2018], no lower than 33.5°C during assessment [BAPM2025], or about 35 °C before hypothermia is started [Ancora2026].

claims.summary: Lower limits differ, with 33°C in CPS guidance [Lemyre2018] and, for axillary temperature, a regional referring-center guideline that also uses 34°C as the upper limit for calling the neonatologist [EasternHealth2022], against 33.5°C in BAPM [BAPM2025]; overcooling during passive cooling is well documented [Kendall2010][Hallberg2009][Mistry2026], and no retrieved source gives a blanket step or a 0.5°C increment.

claims.manual_text: Do not let patients shiver. Counter-warm extremities as needed by wrapping the extremities with a cloth blanket.
claims.summary: Sources differ on shivering in cooled newborns, with one review stating they rarely shiver [McPherson2021] and others describing it during cooling [Joshi2023][Martinello2017]; no studies have systematically evaluated non-pharmacologic treatment for discomfort during cooling [McPherson2021], and no retrieved source addresses counter-warming the extremities.

evidence.quote: Human neonates rely primarily on brown fat thermogenesis to generate body heat during induced hypothermia, and rarely shiver.
evidence.location: Pathophysiology of stress during therapeutic hypothermia; review

evidence.quote: To date, no studies have systematically evaluated non-pharmacologic treatment for discomfort during TH.
evidence.location: Non-pharmacologic approaches to provide comfort during therapeutic hypothermia

evidence.quote: Induced hypothermia is associated with shivering, cold pain, agitation, and distress.
neonates with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy can exhibit hypertonia, tremor, myoclonus and shivering following birth, especially during hypothermia treatment

claims.manual_text: Consider the use of morphine for individual babies who continue to shiver or who are uncomfortable/agitated.
claims.summary: Guidelines recommend opioid treatment for pain or distress in cooled infants [Lemyre2018][BAPM2025], although a Cochrane review found no eligible studies [Backe2022], a large cohort advises cautious empiric use [Natarajan2022] and analgesics can raise the risk of over-cooling [Ancora2026]; these sources concern infants on established cooling, and none studies infants passively cooled before transport.

evidence.quote: Treatment of pain or discomfort during cooling with a low-dose opioid is recommended. Recommendation grade B.
Babies who are cooled should be closely assessed for pain and distress which should be treated with opiate medication if present.

We found no studies that met our inclusion criteria and hence there is no evidence to recommend or refute the use of pharmacological interventions for pain and sedation management in newborn infants undergoing therapeutic hypothermia.
Opioid exposure during TH was not associated with abnormal MRI; its association with adverse short-term outcomes suggests need for cautious empiric use.
sedatives, analgesics, and muscle relaxants can lower body temperature, increasing the risk of over-cooling

claims.manual_text: Obtain IV access. UAC/UVC or PAL access preferred.
claims.summary: BAPM's general care guidance for infants undergoing hypothermia calls for central venous and arterial access [BAPM2025], and most arterial catheters in a North American survey were umbilical [Giesinger2021]; both describe cooling-center care, and no retrieved source addresses referring units.

evidence.quote: Achieve central venous and arterial access.
All infants undergoing TH should have physiological parameters including intra-arterial blood pressure continuously monitored (wherever possible)
Most arterial catheters are placed in a post-ductal position via the umbilical artery (n = 54/57, 94%) route as opposed to a preductal peripheral artery.
evidence.location: Results, Assessment/monitoring of systemic and pulmonary hemodynamics; North American survey

claims.manual_text: **Laboratory / blood work:** ABG (corrected for temperature)
claims.summary: Correcting blood gases to core temperature during cooling is advised [BAPM2025][ElDib2021], and correction lowered PaCO2 values in infants cooled to 33.5°C [Afzal2019]; these sources describe infants being cooled, mainly in cooling centers.

evidence.quote: Aim for normal blood gas values and saturations- avoid hypocarbia /hyperoxia – correct blood gas for patient temperature.
Blood gas values should be corrected to the core temperature during TH and the use of alkaline buffers is discouraged.
Correction of blood gases to patient’s temperature during whole body hypothermia (33.5°C) significantly reduced median (IQR) PaCO2 values from 49 (43–56) to 42 (37–48) mmHg

claims.manual_text: **Laboratory / blood work:** ABG (corrected for temperature), CBC with Diff, Electrolytes, Calcium, Magnesium, Glucose, Blood culture, ALT, AST, BUN, Creatinine, APTT, INR, PT, Lactic Acid, Ammonia, Troponin, and Fibrinogen.
claims.summary: Most of the panel matches first-line bloods for neonatal encephalopathy [Martinello2017] and blood cultures in BAPM guidance [BAPM2025], BAPM names calcium and magnesium for urgent review when seizures are detected [BAPM2025], fibrinogen has a role in predicting bleeding during cooling [Forman2014], but ammonia is listed as second-line in a 2017 narrative review [Martinello2017], troponin evidence is prognostic [Munshi2022], and no retrieved source sets out a complete pre-transport panel.
claims.note: Current evidence suggests, from a 2017 narrative review, that ammonia is a second-line test, to consider when the picture is not typical of HIE [Martinello2017]. Early troponin has been studied as a predictor of residual encephalopathy at discharge in cooled newborns, in a retrospective study [Munshi2022].

evidence.quote: Routine first line bloods are shown in table 1.
evidence.location: First line investigations; table lists full blood count, clotting, direct Coombs test, liver function test, urea and electrolytes, whole blood glucose, blood lactate

evidence.quote: Second line investigations to consider ordering which are available quickly (if concerned this is not typical HIE)

In very sick neonates, ammonia, up to about 110 μmol/L may be present. Very high levels (>200 μmol/L) usually indicate a metabolic cause, for example, urea cycle defect and warrants further investigations.
Take blood cultures and give antibiotics within one hour of birth.
Detection of seizures is an indication for urgent review of blood sodium, glucose, calcium and magnesium.
ROC analyses revealed that platelet count <130 × 109/L, fib level <1.5 g/L, and INR >2 discriminated BG from NBG.
evidence.location: Abstract; BG and NBG are bleeding and non-bleeding groups

evidence.quote: In newborns undergoing TH for HIE, the elevation of troponin within 6 hours of age predicts high risk of having RE at discharge.
evidence.location: Abstract; RE is residual encephalopathy, retrospective

claims.manual_text: **Respiratory support:** Many babies on morphine drip or receiving morphine boluses need some form of respiratory support. This can be obtained through nasal continuous positive airway pressure (with or without a rate) or through invasive mechanical ventilation.
claims.summary: On established cooling, hypoventilation is a common opioid side effect [McPherson2021], almost 90% of opioid-exposed infants in one study were ventilated throughout cooling [Joshi2023], and in another ventilator support rose from baseline in 32% on morphine and none on dexmedetomidine [McPherson2021]; intubation is decided case by case during stabilization and transport [Ancora2026], BAPM's general care guidance bases ventilation on respiratory drive and need for sedation [BAPM2025], and no retrieved source addresses nasal CPAP for infants on morphine or reports respiratory support in infants on morphine during passive cooling before transport.

evidence.quote: These data highlight the common side effects of opioids including hypoventilation, hypotension, urinary retention, and decreased intestinal motility.
evidence.location: Clinical data regarding opioids during therapeutic hypothermia

evidence.quote: Almost 90% of infants exposed to opioids during TH were ventilated for the entire duration of therapy (median 95h)

Approximately half of the study patients in each group required invasive mechanical ventilation, with increased ventilator support from baseline confined exclusively to morphine treated patients (0% vs. 32%, p = 0.02).
evidence.location: Preclinical and clinical data regarding dexmedetomidine during therapeutic hypothermia

evidence.quote: up to 50% of newborns with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy retain spontaneous respiration [56, 61–64]. Therefore, endotracheal intubation should be decided case by case, ensuring hyperoxia and hypocapnia are avoided, as both are associated with adverse outcomes
Intubation and ventilation should be considered to maintain adequate gas exchange depending on the respiratory drive, need for sedation and the ventilatory status.

claims.manual_text: Maintain humidity & temperature of respiratory circuit as standard.
claims.summary: An expert review advises heating inspired gas to 37°C and humidifying it during cooling [ElDib2021], and warmed ventilator gas did not interfere with esophageal temperature readings in cooled infants [Sarkar2015]; both describe infants on established cooling.

evidence.quote: Inspiratory gas should be heated to 37 °C and humidified to prevent airway and alveolar injury.
Warmed inhaled gas does not interfere with the esophageal temperature during WBC.

claims.manual_text: **Medical management as needed:** Including normal saline bolus, vasopressors, acidosis management, blood products, ventilator management, antibiotics,
claims.summary: Each listed support is part of cooled-infant care, with cautions that excessive fluid boluses be avoided and inotropes considered early [BAPM2025], alkaline buffers discouraged [ElDib2021], ventilation managed carefully [Szakmar2019], coagulopathy treated only for active bleeding [BAPM2025], and antibiotics given early in BAPM guidance [BAPM2025] though confirmed early-onset sepsis was very rare in a two-center study [DeRose2025]; these sources describe cooling-center care.

evidence.quote: Aim for BP >45mmHg and treat hypotension according to local guidelines. Avoid excessive fluid boluses and consider inotropes early.
the use of alkaline buffers is discouraged.
Coagulopathy is physiological in TH but only active bleeding needs treatment.
Take blood cultures and give antibiotics within one hour of birth.
The incidence of confirmed early-onset sepsis in neonates with HIE undergoing TH was very low, despite extensive empirical antibiotic use.
judicious ventilatory management with rigorous monitoring is of particular importance in patients with HIE.

claims.manual_text: seizure control (1st choice agent is Phenobarbital).
claims.summary: Phenobarbital is the first-line drug in ILAE guidance regardless of etiology, including HIE [Pressler2023], and in BAPM guidance during cooling [BAPM2025], and it was more effective than levetiracetam in a randomized trial [Sharpe2020]; the 2026 Italian guideline lists phenobarbital and phenytoin as first-line [Ancora2026].

evidence.quote: In neonates with seizures requiring ASM, phenobarbital should be the first- line ASM.
Phenobarbital should be the first- line ASM regardless of etiology (including HIE, stroke, and hemorrhage).
Use intravenous phenobarbital as first line treatment in babies undergoing TH, in a dose of 20 mg/kg given over 20 minutes.
In this study conducted in the hypothermia era and with near real-time response to continuous video EEG monitoring, phenobarbital was more effective than levetiracetam in achieving seizure cessation.
Phenobarbital and phenytoin are first-line treatments, with additional options including benzodiazepines, lidocaine, topiramate, and levetiracetam.

omissions.note: Current evidence suggests a low infusion of morphine (≤10 mcg/kg/h) or equivalent opioid as the initial approach during cooling; higher rates were associated with toxic serum levels in a subset of infants in one study [Lemyre2018].

evidence.quote: A low infusion of morphine (≤10 mcg/kg/h) or equivalent opioid is recommended as the initial approach for easing discomfort.
Infusions of morphine at rates higher than 10 mcg/kg/hour have been associated with toxic serum levels in a subset of infants enrolled in one study (43).

known_limitations: Zanelli2026 (AAP 2026 clinical report) and Lee2025 were not read in full after logged access refusals; Zanelli2026 was read as an abstract only, and AAPNews2026 is a lay news item, so AAP specifics on passive cooling, temperature and exclusions remain unchecked.
Evidence for morphine and supportive care (c23-c25, c27-c29) comes from infants on established cooling; rulings state the setting.
BAPM2025 is listed in scope.set_aside for its mild-HIE section only and stays cited for the 35-week point.
